paper.title: Predicting silent failures of learned inference under restricted access: what measurement physics and prior information explain
paper.abstract: Abstract Learned priors are used to reconstruct regions that measurements barely reach, and to report uncertainty there. They can fail silently: the reported interval excludes the truth while every ground-truth-free diagnostic stays within its noise. We call such errors the blind set and ask whether they can be predicted before the target data are seen. For a correctly specified linear-Gaussian model averaged over the prior, the risk of a silent failure factorises exactly into non-detection and non-coverage, which does not hold for learned systems in general; we build a score that approximates this reference by linearising a VAE prior. In a prospective study on real X-ray CT objects (2DeteCT) under simulated restricted access, with predictions committed by hash before any trial, the score ranked the realised blindness of two learned inference systems (latent Laplace and ensemble Kalman inversion) with Spearman ρ = 0.79 \rho=0.79 and 0.84 0.84 over 240 pre-specified errors. Simple structural predictors would also have passed these tests. Sequential post-hoc analyses, each specified before its own computation, show that under bounded reach the learned score gave no detectable improvement over a physics-based baseline, in rankings or trial-level log scores. At the weakest attenuation studied, prior information improved rankings over the physics-based baseline, most clearly for ensemble Kalman inversion, but a Gaussian prior did as well and the gain was not detectable at the trial level. The score is not a calibrated probability. Silent failures can be anticipated here, but their structure follows mainly from measurement access and the decision quantity rather than from the learned prior.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Reconstructing what cannot be observed directly, such as the interior of a sealed component or a region a sensor cannot reach, is increasingly done with learned priors [ 4 ] , and decisions are taken on the uncertainty these systems report. Such a system can fail in two ways. It can be uncertain and say so: its reported uncertainty is wide where its evidence is thin. Or it can be confidently wrong : the reported uncertainty excludes the truth, while every check it can run without ground truth (residuals, consistency across measurement subsets, plausibility of the fitted latent state) stays within its noise. The second failure looks, from inside the system, exactly like a well-supported inference. Each ingredient of this failure is established. Misspecification that the data cannot detect can be bounded or made harmless to estimators [ 11 , 2 ] ; prior-data conflict checks find misspecification that does reach the data [ 7 ] . Priors mismatched to the truth can destroy the coverage of credible sets in inverse problems [ 15 , 10 ] , including under partial observation [ 9 ] . Learned reconstructions can place false structure in components the measurements do not determine [ 3 ] ; learned uncertainty degrades under distribution shift [ 16 ] ; conformal methods guarantee coverage only on average and under exchangeability [ 1 ] ; and misspecified models can be precise yet inaccurate with little residual warning [ 5 ] . What is not established is whether the conjunction —errors both undetected and outside the reported uncertainty—can be predicted in advance for a learned non-linear system, from the model, the operator, the diagnostic suite and the noise alone. The blind set differs from each of these notions: non-coverage alone may be flagged by a diagnostic, an undetectable perturbation may leave the decision quantity unchanged, and prior-data conflict concerns misfit that the data do reveal. The blind set is their intersection, defined for a stated decision quantity and diagnostic suite. We separate three claims: (a) blind errors can be predicted prospectively; (b) local linearisation of learned inference provides an effective predictor; (c) learned-prior geometry contributes information that simpler predictors lack. The evidence supports (a) in the tested setting, gives qualified support to (b), and does not establish (c) (Section 8 ). The pre-specified tests show that a score computed before any trial ranks realised blindness. They do not separate it from structural baselines: the indicator of the unreached region and the error’s effect on the decision quantity alone reach Spearman ρ = 0.52 \rho=0.52 –0.66 and 0.57–0.70 under bounded reach, so they too would have met the pre-specified threshold. Everything we conclude about what makes blindness predictable comes from sequential post-hoc analyses, each specified in writing before its own computation but designed with earlier results known (Table 1 ). Linear-Gaussian pilots of the blind set are reported in a companion technical note [ 8 ] ; the present paper does not rely on them. Our contributions are of three kinds, which we keep apart. 1. Formulation and reference. The blind set and its population-averaged risk (Section 2 ), and an exact result for the linear-Gaussian case (Proposition 1 ): averaged over the prior, non-detection and non-coverage are independent for any detector, and the posterior spread is the correct scale. The result follows from a standard property of Gaussian conditioning; what it adds is its application to the blindness risk. 2. A computational procedure. A prospective risk-ranking score that approximates this reference by linearising a learned prior (Section 3 ). We offer no new theory of why learned uncertainty fails. 3. Empirical findings about which information suffices to anticipate silent failure under different access regimes (Sections 5 – 7 ): a prospective test on real CT objects with two learned inference systems; comparisons with physics-based, Gaussian and structural predictors at the level of rankings and of individual trials; and a full record of what was fixed when, of failed configurations and of deviations (Appendix A ). Part of what we observe follows directly from the measurement null space, the size of an error and the sensitivity of the decision quantity; Proposition 1 makes this precise. The experiments add what does not follow from these alone: how often calibrated learned systems were silently wrong beyond reach; that, at the level of individual trials, the learned score gave no detectable predictive improvement over a physics-based score; that under weak but non-zero access prior information improves rankings, though not in a way specific to the learned prior nor as a detectable gain in trial-level predictive performance; and that a score computed before any target data, from a single surrogate, ranked the blindness of two different inference algorithms.

sections.heading: Objects.
sections.text: We use the high-fidelity (mode 2) reference reconstructions of 2DeteCT [ 14 ] , slices 1–2000, block-mean downsampled to 64 × 64 64\times 64 and multiplied by 100. Consecutive slices image the same sample tube and are strongly correlated, so a contiguous split is not exchangeable (Appendix A ). We split by interleaved 10-slice blocks (index ≡ 4 ( mod 10 ) \equiv 4\pmod{10} for calibration, ≡ 9 \equiv 9 for testing, the rest for training), removing from training the two slices either side of every held-out block: 1,442 training, 200 calibration and 200 test slices. Every sample tube therefore contributes to training and to testing. The 750 out-of-distribution slices of 2DeteCT (figs, nuts, titanium screws and other objects absent from the training mixtures) are used only to build errors.

sections.text: Measurements are simulated with a parallel-beam CT operator (60 angles over 180 ∘ 180^{\circ} , 64 bins; 3,840 rays) with Gaussian noise of standard deviation σ 0 \sigma_{0} equal to 1% of the RMS projection. Under bounded reach , every ray through a hidden disc R R (radius 7 px) is removed, so R R lies exactly in the null space of the operator (Fig. 1 a,b; m = 2,891 m=2{,}891 rays kept, 2,896 in the second geometry). sections.heading: Learned prior.
sections.text: A convolutional VAE [ 13 ] with latent dimension 32 (encoder: four stride-2 4 × 4 4\times 4 convolutions with 32, 64, 128, 128 channels and a 256-unit dense layer; decoder: dense layers to 4 × 4 × 128 4\times 4\times 128 , four nearest-neighbour upsampling and 3 × 3 3\times 3 convolution stages with 128, 64, 32, 16 channels; GELU) is trained on the training slices with the eight symmetries of the square (2,000 Adam steps, batch 64, cosine-decayed learning rate from 10 − 3 10^{-3} , decoder noise 0.05). The KL weight rose linearly from 0 to 1 over the whole run, reaching 1 only at the last step, so the encoder’s aggregate posterior need not match 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , I ) \mathcal{N}(0,I) . The decoder is imperfect, and we model its error as a stationary Gaussian field whose covariance is the radially averaged power spectrum of the decoder residuals on the calibration slices (16 parameters), giving Σ y = A ​ C pix ​ A ⊤ + diag ⁡ ( σ i 2 ) \Sigma_{y}=A\,C_{\mathrm{pix}}A^{\top}+\mathrm{diag}(\sigma_{i}^{2}) and the bias (0.0004) and standard deviation (0.017) of the model error in q q . Stationarity is an assumption, since decoder errors concentrate near object edges; it was chosen because a rank-60 empirical covariance over-fitted the detector null (Appendix A ).

sections.heading: Inference systems.
sections.text: (i) VAE-Laplace : latent MAP by damped Gauss–Newton (up to 30 iterations) with a Laplace approximation in latent space. It is warm-started from the encoder applied to the Gaussian-baseline posterior mean, which couples the two systems; a cold start was not tested. (ii) VAE-EKI : ensemble Kalman inversion in latent space [ 12 ] , ES-MDA form [ 6 ] , 200 members, four steps with inflation α i = 4 \alpha_{i}=4 , so that ∑ i α i − 1 = 1 \sum_{i}\alpha_{i}^{-1}=1 . (iii) Gaussian baseline : the exact linear-Gaussian posterior under the empirical mean and a rank-200 covariance of the training images, plus an isotropic term whose variance is that of the training images’ residual outside the rank-200 subspace; it shows what access and a generic prior alone imply. Each system reports a 95% interval for q q as estimate ± 1.96 ​ κ \pm 1.96\,\kappa times its spread (for EKI, the standard deviation of the ensemble’s values of q q , an ensemble-derived rather than an exact Bayesian interval). The factor κ \kappa is set separately for each system and each decision quantity, on the calibration slices, so that coverage there is 95%. This is an empirical adjustment of marginal coverage; it does not guarantee coverage conditional on an object, a perturbation or a shift in distribution. Before calibration every system was overconfident for the unreached quantity even on ordinary slices: raw coverage of q q was 0.685, 0.718 and 0.708 ( κ = 2.08 \kappa=2.08 , 2.32, 2.24), against 0.99, 0.985 and 0.74 for the within-reach control.

sections.heading: Diagnostics.
sections.text: Nine ground-truth-free diagnostics: the standardised whitened total residual T 0 T_{0} , six angle-block residuals, latent typicality ‖ z ^ ‖ 2 \|\hat{z}\|^{2} (VAE systems only) and the lag-1 residual autocorrelation along the detector. They are combined in a Mahalanobis detector with mean, covariance and 5% false-alarm threshold set on the calibration slices (empirical null): nine retained diagnostics (null covariance of rank 8) and t = 20.9 t=20.9 (Laplace), 20.3 20.3 (EKI); eight (rank 7) and t = 15.6 t=15.6 for the Gaussian system, which has no typicality term (main study; other studies are in the deposited calibration files). On the test slices without errors, false alarms were 3.0%, 3.5% and 3.5%, and coverage of q q was 0.93, 0.945 and 0.985; the Gaussian system’s over-coverage lowers its own blind rate on ordinary slices.

sections.heading: Errors.
sections.text: The error set has 240 members: inclusions of radius 2 or 3 px with amplitude + 0.3 +0.3 , + 0.8 +0.8 , + 1.5 +1.5 or − 0.15 -0.15 (a void; inclusions are clipped at zero, while the score uses the unclipped δ \delta , so for voids on near-zero bases the score is, if anything, too high), at six positions in each of four classes— in R R (centre within 4 px of R R ’s centre), adjacent (centre 10–13 px from it), in C C , and elsewhere within reach—and 48 transplants of radius-5 discs of real out-of-distribution content, 12 per class. Radius-5 transplants in the first two classes can extend up to 2 px across R R ’s boundary. In units of the prior standard deviation of q q ( σ q = 0.041 \sigma_{q}=0.041 ), inclusions in R R shift q q by a median of 0.5 (voids), 1.0, 2.8 and 5.2 (amplitudes + 0.3 +0.3 , + 0.8 +0.8 , + 1.5 +1.5 ), and transplants by 2.3; in units of the mean uninflated Laplace spread these are 1.2–11.6 and 5.1. All errors outside R R leave q q unchanged ( c ⊤ ​ δ = 0 c^{\top}\delta=0 ) except transplants that reach across its boundary. The largest perturbations are thus far outside the range of q q on ordinary slices (mean about 0.11).

sections.heading: Studies.
sections.text: The main study (Main) applies each error to five fixed test slices with two noise draws (10 trials per error). A robustness study, fixed before its trials, used 20 test slices per study with common random numbers (each slice run with and without each error under the same noise draw) and the excess blind rate over the slice’s own blindness as outcome: A1 repeats the main set-up; A2 moves the hidden disc and recalibrates; A3 uses attenuated access at F = 128,000 F=128{,}000 , with a central decision disc and the four classes replaced by depth rings by distance from the tube centre. Post-hoc analyses added A3 at F = 32,000 F=32{,}000 and 512,000 512{,}000 (10 slices each). A2 and A3 used 120 errors at alternate positions.

sections.heading: What was fixed when.
sections.text: Table 1 summarises the hierarchy of evidence. Predictions and decision criteria of the main study were fixed, and the prediction file hashed (SHA-256), before any trial; the robustness study was fixed before its trials; seven post-hoc analysis plans were each written and approved before their own computation, after earlier results were known. The plans, hashes, deviations and failed configurations are in Appendix A and the deposited records. sections.heading: Prospective tests.
sections.text: The main study’s criteria were: H1 , Spearman ρ \rho between S blind S_{\mathrm{blind}} and the realised blind rate over the 240 errors ≥ 0.5 \geq 0.5 , with an interval excluding zero; H1b , the same within R R (60 errors), ρ ≥ 0.3 \rho\geq 0.3 ; H2 , the learned score ranks realised blindness better than the Gaussian prediction. All were met (Table 2 , Fig. 2 ). Inclusions inside R R cannot move any diagnostic, since A ​ δ = 0 A\delta=0 ; they never raised the learned systems’ detectors, and VAE-Laplace missed them confidently in 53% of trials (transplants, 55%). Within R R , blindness rose with amplitude: realised 0.35, 0.71 and 0.87 for + 0.3 +0.3 , + 0.8 +0.8 , + 1.5 +1.5 (mean scores 0.22, 0.71, 0.95), and 0.20 for voids (mean score 0.09). In the reference H1b is guaranteed by design (Proposition 1 (ii)); in the realised systems such errors leave the data unchanged, so only their effect on q q varies, and within R R the Gaussian prediction ranks errors about as well as the learned one ( ρ = 0.959 \rho=0.959 against 0.948 for Laplace). The structural predictors alone would also have met H1’s threshold (Table 3 ), and H2 used the Gaussian prediction, which is a weak comparator under bounded reach. sections.heading: Trial-level analysis.
sections.text: Spearman ρ \rho over a designed error set depends on how the set was built, and each realised rate rests on 10 or 20 trials. We therefore also modelled the blind indicator of every trial (Table 4 ). Under bounded reach the learned and physics-based scores had the same discrimination (AUROC 0.78–0.95, within 0.01 of each other), above the region indicator (0.70–0.87). Each improved the cross-validated log score of a structural model (region indicator and rank of | c ⊤ ​ δ | |c^{\top}\delta| , with base-slice intercepts) by 0.06–0.09 nats per trial. The intervals in Table 4 refit every model in every fold of every bootstrap replicate (seventh plan). With them, these gains were above zero in four of the six bounded-reach pairs but not for EKI in Main and A1, where intervals that did not refit had excluded zero; the change is marginal (lower limits moved from + 0.005 +0.005 – + 0.023 +0.023 to − 0.005 -0.005 – − 0.021 -0.021 ). Neither score improved detectably on the other: the gain from adding the learned score to a model that already contains the physics-based one was between − 0.002 -0.002 and 0.000 in every bounded-reach pair, with refitted upper limits of at most 0.016 nats per trial, and, by the rule fixed in advance, no incremental improvement from the learned score beyond the physics-based score was detected in any of the twelve study–system pairs without refitting, or in any of the ten whose refitted intervals are interpretable (nor from physics beyond the learned score). At F = 512,000 F=512{,}000 the refitted intervals are orders of magnitude wider than elsewhere and are marked not interpretable: blindness there is confined almost entirely to the deepest ring, and the refitted models appear to separate, or nearly separate, the outcomes in some replicates, giving a few held-out trials extreme log scores (Table 4 ). Across 101 random partitions of the errors into folds, this gain varied by at most 0.006 under bounded reach, well within its interval. No equivalence margin was fixed in advance, so this is an absence of detected improvement, not a demonstration that the two scores carry the same information; descriptively, the refitted upper limits are at most about a fifth of either score’s gain over the structural model. The folds hold out errors, not base slices or objects: all trials of an error, on every base slice, are left out together, and the base-slice intercepts and coefficients are refitted on the remaining errors in each fold. Unlike the prospective score, these models are fitted to realised outcomes. The gains therefore measure the incremental information each score carries for unseen errors on the same base slices; they do not estimate performance on new objects without outcome-based fitting. The seventh plan also held out base slices, grouped by CT block, together with the errors, replacing the slice intercepts by a common one (Table 10 ). The learned score again added no detectable information beyond physics in any pair, and either score improved the structural model with an interval above zero for A1 Laplace and A2 only. In the main study five slices were too few for this design: the structural model predicted unseen slices poorly (mean log score − 0.94 -0.94 and − 2.66 -2.66 nats per trial, against − 0.23 -0.23 and − 0.13 -0.13 with slice intercepts), and the intervals were very wide. Held-out slices come from the same sample tubes as the training slices, so this is not validation on independent objects. The calibration slope and intercept of the learned score (models without base-slice terms, fitted to all trials) had intervals containing 1 and 0 in five of the six bounded-reach pairs, the exception being A1 Laplace. With five base slices these intervals are wide (slope [0.37, 1.85] for Main Laplace); they fail to reject calibration rather than show it, and calibration-in-the-large remains − 0.08 -0.08 to − 0.09 -0.09 in the main study (Section 7 ). sections.heading: Rankings after adjustment.
sections.text: Two measures adjust for properties of the errors and answer different questions (Table 5 ). The stratified ρ \rho asks whether a predictor ranks errors within groups of similar errors (strata of location class × \times error kind × \times amplitude; ranks centred within strata, Pearson correlation of the pooled centred ranks; strata with fewer than three errors dropped). The partial ρ \rho converts prediction and outcome to ranks, regresses each by least squares on an intercept, the rank of | c ⊤ ​ δ | |c^{\top}\delta| and the region indicator, and correlates the residuals; it adjusts for one binary feature of location only. Both use average ranks for ties and are recomputed, regressions included, in every bootstrap replicate. Under bounded reach the learned and physics-based scores showed no detectable difference on either measure: v1 − - physics was − 0.08 -0.08 to + 0.01 +0.01 in partial ρ \rho and − 0.18 -0.18 to + 0.07 +0.07 in stratified ρ \rho , with every two-way interval including zero. Counted separately against the rule fixed in the third plan (stratified or partial interval excluding zero), the learned score met this rule for information beyond these variables in all six bounded-reach pairs and the physics-based baseline in three, but this asymmetry rests on lower interval limits that differ by hundredths while the point estimates are nearly equal or favour physics; it is not evidence of a difference. The Gaussian prediction did not (partial ρ ≤ 0.13 \rho\leq 0.13 ). The main-study intervals are strongly skewed: leaving out one of its five base slices lowered the partial ρ \rho of both scores to near zero (0.08 and 0.01 for Laplace, 0.01 and 0.02 for EKI), while leaving out any other slice changed little and the stratified ρ \rho stayed at 0.25–0.42; one slice drives the main-study partial ρ \rho . To control location within the reached region, the fifth plan added a natural cubic spline in the distance to the unreached disc (Table 9 ): within reach, the two scores’ point estimates were again nearly identical (for example 0.69 and 0.69 for Main Laplace) and their difference included zero everywhere, while the learned score’s interval excluded zero in five of six pairs and the physics-based baseline’s in one. At F = 512,000 F=512{,}000 almost all within-reach outcomes are zero, and these values are not interpretable (Table 9 ). The two scores agree closely but not perfectly: their rank correlation across errors is 0.84 under bounded reach (0.62–0.64 within reach) and 0.42–0.59 under attenuation, so their similar trial-level performance is an empirical finding rather than a consequence of identical scores. These are statistical findings, not a mechanism. The physics-based baseline’s only remaining input after adjustment is ‖ A w ​ δ ‖ 2 \|A_{w}\delta\|^{2} , the error’s detectability in the whitened measurements, which suggests that detectability carries the residual information, but its wider intervals do not let us say that it carries all of it.

sections.heading: Access explains much of the blind set.
sections.text: The Gaussian system was itself confidently wrong for errors beyond reach in 44% (Main), 30% (A1), 28% (A2) and 40% (A3) of trials. Under bounded reach, which errors are blind is predicted by access, the measurement physics and the decision quantity; the learned prior mainly sets how often blindness occurs on ordinary images, through the overconfidence that calibration had to correct.

sections.heading: What predicts blindness.
sections.text: At F = 128,000 F=128{,}000 the pre-specified score met H1 and H2 for EKI but not for Laplace (Appendix A ). Across strengths (Table 3 ), at the weakest attenuation, F = 32,000 F=32{,}000 , the learned score ranked realised blindness better than the physics-based baseline for EKI (v1 − - physics + 0.30 +0.30 [0.033, 0.480]); for Laplace the interval reached zero ( + 0.26 +0.26 [ − 0.004 -0.004 , 0.418]), and the physics-based baseline carried almost no information within reach ( ρ ≈ 0.01 \rho\approx 0.01 ). After adjustment for effect size and region, the learned score again ranked better than physics for EKI at this strength (partial ρ \rho difference + 0.56 +0.56 [0.071, 0.821]), consistent with the unadjusted result; at 512,000 512{,}000 three adjusted differences exclude zero, with mixed sign (partial ρ \rho : + 0.14 +0.14 Laplace, + 0.05 +0.05 EKI; stratified ρ \rho : − 0.01 -0.01 EKI; Table 5 ). This was not specific to the learned prior: the Gaussian prediction ranked realised blindness at least as well (0.64 and 0.73 against 0.59 and 0.69), and at no strength did the learned score beat it with a two-way interval excluding zero (at F = 128,000 F=128{,}000 , where EKI met H2 with an error-only interval of [0.015, 0.238], the two-way interval was [ − 0.064 -0.064 , 0.234]). At 512,000 512{,}000 , where blindness was confined to the deepest ring, all predictions ranked errors alike (EKI: 0.66 each) and the region indicator did better (0.79). At the trial level (Table 4 ) the learned score improved the structural model at F = 128,000 F=128{,}000 for both systems but not at 32,000 32{,}000 (at 512,000 512{,}000 the refitted log-score intervals are not interpretable), and nowhere did it add detectable information beyond the physics-based score (at F = 32,000 F=32{,}000 the gains were + 0.020 +0.020 and + 0.035 +0.035 nats per trial, with intervals including zero); its AUROC exceeded the physics-based score’s by 0.05–0.07 at F = 32,000 F=32{,}000 and by 0.04 for EKI at 128,000 128{,}000 , with intervals reaching down to about zero. Following the rule fixed in the second plan, we describe a learned-prior contribution under attenuation as open rather than absent. Rank correlation across errors and trial-level log score measure different things: the first, how well errors are ordered by blind rate; the second, how well individual trials are predicted. At the weakest attenuation prior information improved the ordering of errors, but this did not appear as a detectable gain in probabilistic prediction beyond the physics-based score.

sections.heading: Taking calibration out of the comparison.
sections.text: Because each system’s κ \kappa was tuned separately, the fifth plan recomputed realised blindness and both predictions with κ = 1 \kappa=1 for every system. Under bounded reach the learned score then ranked realised blindness better than the Gaussian prediction by + 0.32 +0.32 to + 0.44 +0.44 (all intervals excluding zero); under attenuation the two did not differ (for EKI at F = 128,000 F=128{,}000 , + 0.09 +0.09 [ − 0.06 -0.06 , 0.19], against + 0.12 +0.12 with calibrated intervals). Against the physics-based baseline with κ = 1 \kappa=1 (sixth plan) the learned score ranked no better: v1 − - physics ranged from − 0.27 -0.27 to + 0.17 +0.17 , physics was ahead in most pairs, and no two-way interval excluded zero except a negligible one at F = 512,000 F=512{,}000 for EKI ( − 0.001 -0.001 ).

sections.heading: The reference, numerically.
sections.text: Under the linearised model at the same 100 points, with objects drawn from the prior and the detector’s null recalibrated on error-free draws (false alarms 5%), the joint and product probabilities differed by at most 0.002 for every error, and Monte Carlo and analytic non-coverage at κ = 1 \kappa=1 by at most 0.006, in every study. Since Proposition 1 guarantees this agreement, the check verifies the implementation rather than providing independent evidence. An earlier Monte Carlo version (third plan), which drew only noise around the linearisation point (no variation of the object and no shrinkage bias) and inherited a detector null that the linearised diagnostics did not reproduce (23–45% false alarms on error-free draws), ranked realised blindness worse than S blind S_{\mathrm{blind}} . The prior-averaged version with the recalibrated null showed no detectable difference from it under bounded reach (differences − 0.16 -0.16 to − 0.01 -0.01 , every two-way interval including zero). This is consistent with the deficit arising from the noise-only simulation and the mismatched null, which met the rule fixed in the fifth plan; but the two changes were made together, so it cannot be assigned to either alone, and no detected difference is not equivalence. Under attenuation the prior-averaged version still ranked worse at F = 32,000 F=32{,}000 ( − 0.27 -0.27 and − 0.25 -0.25 ; interval excluding zero for Laplace) and alike at 512,000 512{,}000 . A first computation of this check inverted a singular null covariance (the total-residual diagnostic is a linear combination of the six block residuals); the corrected computation uses a pseudo-inverse, as the realised detector does, and both are logged in the deposited records.

sections.heading: Components and dependence.
sections.text: The fourth plan compared each component with its realised counterpart (Appendix B ). The analytic detection component ranked realised alarm rates in every study and system ( ρ = 0.54 \rho=0.54 –0.94) and was within ± 0.05 \pm 0.05 of them on average in 5 of 12 pairs; a Monte Carlo version ranked them as well but exceeded them by 0.32–0.54. The calibrated posterior spread described realised non-coverage better than the sampling variability of the linearised estimator in 9 of 12 pairs, as Proposition 1 leads one to expect for rates averaged over slices. In the realised systems, per-error blind rates differed little from the product of their realised non-detection and non-coverage rates (mean difference − 0.021 -0.021 to + 0.009 +0.009 ), but not little enough in ranking to meet the rule fixed in advance for calling the events independent ( ρ \rho below 0.95 in 6 of 12 pairs). Swapping one component at a time, a sensitivity analysis rather than a causal decomposition, showed that neither component alone accounts for the analytic score’s advantage over the Monte Carlo version: the coverage component mattered under bounded reach and the detection component under attenuation. Figure 4: Reliability of the scores against the raw blind rate (third post-hoc plan), for the learned (v1), Gaussian and physics-based predictions; bins of score, observed rate with two-way bootstrap 95% intervals; dashed line: perfect calibration.

sections.heading: Calibration.
sections.text: S blind S_{\mathrm{blind}} is not a calibrated probability (Fig. 4 ). Its calibration-in-the-large (mean score minus observed rate; Table 8 ), which checks only the average level, ranged from − 0.09 -0.09 (main study) to + 0.13 +0.13 (strongest attenuation), outside the ± 0.05 \pm 0.05 fixed in advance. At the trial level its calibration slope was 0.31–0.58 at F = 32,000 F=32{,}000 and 128,000 128{,}000 (scores too spread out) and 2.4–2.7 at 512,000 512{,}000 (too compressed). Its Brier score showed no detectable difference from the physics-based baseline’s under bounded reach (differences − 0.0007 -0.0007 to + 0.0001 +0.0001 , every two-way interval including zero; deposited results of the third plan). Its Brier differences from the Gaussian prediction, negative under bounded reach and positive under attenuation, are in Table 8 . Part of the level error comes from the detection law: with ν = 9 \nu=9 at the empirical thresholds, the χ 2 \chi^{2} law implies false-alarm rates of 1.2–2.2% under bounded reach and 6–9% under attenuation rather than the empirical 5%, shifting non-detection by a roughly constant amount. Recomputing the score with ν \nu equal to the rank (8) and t t the 95% quantile of χ 8 2 \chi^{2}_{8} (sixth plan) changed ρ \rho by − 0.03 -0.03 to + 0.03 +0.03 , every interval including zero, and calibration-in-the-large by at most 0.01; the ranking is insensitive to this choice.

sections.heading: Population and linearisation points.
sections.text: The test slices lie far outside the typical set of the latent prior: the squared norm of their encoder means averaged 66.5 (5–95%: 30.8–104.4), against 32 (20.1–46.2) under χ 32 2 \chi^{2}_{32} (Kolmogorov–Smirnov distance 0.80), consistent with the KL weight reaching 1 only at the end of training. S blind S_{\mathrm{blind}} therefore averages local sensitivities over objects unlike the test population, which may contribute to its miscalibration. Strong shrinkage of such objects towards the prior is also a plausible cause of the systems’ overconfidence for the unreached quantity, which required κ ≈ 2 \kappa\approx 2 (Section 4 ); we have not tested this. Its ranking was nonetheless stable: 25 or 50 linearisation points instead of 100 changed ρ \rho by at most 0.05, and points taken from encoded training images by − 0.09 -0.09 to + 0.02 +0.02 . Stability shows that the ranking does not hinge on a few points or on where they are drawn; it does not show that the linearisations reproduce the non-linear systems. One reading, consistent with the physics-based baseline’s performance, is that the ranking is dominated by quantities that change little across z k z_{k} : the whitened operator acting on δ \delta and the decision functional. Scaling κ \kappa from 0.75 to 1.5 times its calibrated value lowered the blind rate in R R from about 0.65 to 0.40 in the main study while ρ \rho stayed between 0.73 and 0.85. A physics baseline with no VAE-derived input ranked realised blindness lower than the physics-based baseline by 0.14–0.19 in five of the six bounded-reach study–system pairs and 0.02 higher in the sixth (A1, Laplace; Table 8 ), with every two-way interval for the difference including zero; by the rule fixed in the third plan we attribute the bounded-reach agreement to measurement structure, but without the model-error whitening every within-reach error is deemed certainly detected, so the within-reach part depends on modelling the decoder’s error.

sections.heading: A use of the score.
sections.text: Before any target data are seen, one can flag the errors the system cannot vouch for. In every study a quarter of the errors lie in the unreached region (or deepest ring), so a budget of 25% coincides with the design: flagging the top quarter by S blind S_{\mathrm{blind}} captured 55–91% of blind trials under bounded reach and 45–100% under attenuation, with precision (the blind rate among flagged trials) 0.43–0.59 and 0.30–0.54, and the region indicator gave nearly the same flags. Across budgets from 5% to 50% (sixth plan), precision fell from 0.92–1.00 at 5% to 0.22–0.39 at 50% under bounded reach, and the learned flag captured more blind trials than the physics-based flag in none of 120 budget × \times study–system combinations. These capture and precision values are conditional on the constructed error set: the share of errors placed in the unreached region, and with it the prevalence of blind errors, was fixed by design. They show that the score can prioritise errors within this setting, not how well it would detect defects in operation, which would need a model of the errors expected in deployment. Its value here comes from access and effect size.

sections.heading: 8 Discussion and limitations
sections.text: (a) Blind errors can be predicted prospectively: supported in the tested setting. A score computed before the target data ranked which errors learned non-linear inference missed without warning, in two bounded-reach geometries for both learned systems and under attenuated access for the ensemble system. The pre-specified tests do not show that anything beyond access and effect size is needed for this. (b) Local linearisation of learned inference provides an effective predictor: qualified support. The score approximates an exact linear-Gaussian reference, ranked blindness well and identified detectable errors, but it is not a calibrated probability, it averages over a prior that does not describe the test population, and an exact Monte Carlo evaluation of the local model showed no detectable difference from the score under bounded reach and ranked worse at the weakest attenuation. (c) Learned-prior geometry contributes information that simpler predictors lack: not established. Under bounded reach the learned score showed no detectable advantage over the physics-based baseline in rankings, adjusted rankings or trial-level log scores; with no equivalence margin fixed in advance, this does not show that the two carry identical information. At the weakest attenuation studied, prior information improved rank correlations over the physics-based baseline, but a Gaussian prior did as well, and the improvement in ranking did not appear as a detectable gain in trial-level log score beyond physics. Whether a learned prior adds stable structure where data and prior trade off continuously remains open.

sections.heading: What is established, approximated and observed.
sections.text: Three levels of statement should be kept apart. Exact: for a correctly specified linear-Gaussian model averaged over the prior, non-detection and non-coverage are independent and the risk factorises (Proposition 1 ). Approximate: the score applies this product to local linearisations of a non-linear system, with an inflation factor fitted for coverage, a one-component detection law and an average over prior draws (Section 3 ); it is checked numerically only against its own linearised model. Empirical: in the realised systems, per-error blind rates were close on average to the product of realised non-detection and non-coverage, but not close enough in ranking to meet the rule fixed for calling the events independent, and trial-level odds ratios were imprecise (Section 7 ); independence in the realised systems is neither established nor excluded. The contribution is therefore an empirical and methodological investigation of which information suffices to anticipate silent failure, supported by an exact Gaussian reference; it is neither a general theory of uncertainty failure nor a demonstration that learned priors predict it better. Much of the structure of the blind set follows from measurement access and the decision quantity, as Proposition 1 predicts for the null space; prior information improved rankings at the weakest attenuation studied. Across the three attenuation strengths we observed a consistent pattern, which we present as an observation in this setting: as access weakened towards none, the blind set changed from a graded profile to an edge, the reported uncertainty beyond reach went from honest on average to overconfident, and the learned, Gaussian and physics-based predictions converged as blindness became dominated by location. The Laplace approximation was the weaker system throughout.

sections.heading: Calibration and the practical message.
sections.text: Interval inflation was already set per decision quantity, so the unreached quantity had its own κ \kappa ; even so, every system needed κ ≈ 2 \kappa\approx 2 –2.3 there on ordinary slices. Region-wise or conformal recalibration on ordinary slices may improve marginal coverage under the relevant calibration assumptions, but it does not guarantee coverage for atypical perturbations in regions that the measurements do not constrain, which is where the blind set lives: inclusions in R R moved q q by up to five prior standard deviations. This is the conditional-shift failure of prior-dominated quantities known in the linear setting [ 15 , 10 ] ; the score’s use is to say in advance which perturbations a deployed system cannot vouch for.

sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: The pre-specified score models detection through the total residual only; one score serves both learned systems; the physics-based baseline uses the decoder’s model-error covariance and the Laplace spread. Seventeen pre-specified criteria per system were evaluated without multiplicity correction, and the pre-specified intervals resample errors only. Images are 64 × 64 64\times 64 and measurements are simulated, with Gaussian rather than Poisson noise under attenuation. There is one data source, one VAE (latent dimension 32, one training run, warm-started Laplace fits) and one scalar decision quantity, so failures of shape, topology or small features are untested. Errors are inclusions, voids and transplants at chosen locations; attenuation was studied at three strengths. Variation is resampled across noise draws and base slices but not across physical objects: the interleaved split places every sample tube in training and testing, so object-level resampling is not possible with these data. The objects are real CT reference reconstructions, but the restricted-access measurements were simulated from them; no measurement was acquired under the access conditions studied. The conclusions refer to the two inference systems, the slices of the 2DeteCT sample tubes, the error classes and the simulated access conditions studied; validation on independently acquired objects and real restricted-access measurements is needed before any wider claim. Natural next steps are a second decision quantity, recorded sinograms with Poisson noise, independent objects, richer priors, system-specific predictors for ensemble methods, the physics-based baseline as a standard comparator, and measurement design aimed at shrinking the blind set.

sections.heading: Pre-specification.
sections.text: Predictions, decision criteria, thresholds and outcome interpretations were fixed in a dated analysis plan; the prediction file was hashed (SHA-256) and the plan finalised by the author before any realised trial. The plans, their dates and the hashes are recorded in a dated project log and in freeze logs written by the pipeline, but not with an external registry; we therefore describe the study as pre-specified and committed by hash before trials . Deviations affecting the main study were a crash fix in the control run and a restart with single-threaded libraries (both before any result was inspected), and an erratum found later: the plan described the model-error covariance as “rank 60 plus diagonal”, whereas the frozen code (whose hash was recorded) used the 16-parameter spectrum. These are pre-specified decision criteria, not formal tests of the null hypothesis ρ < 0.5 \rho<0.5 . Before freezing, each learned system had to show at most 15% false alarms and at least 85% coverage of q q on the test slices without errors.

New criteria: H4 , within reach, ρ \rho (score, excess) ≥ 0.3 \geq 0.3 and greater than the Gaussian prediction’s; H5 , within R R , the learned score has smaller mean absolute error than the Gaussian prediction against the raw blind rate; H6 (attenuation), excess blindness decreases from the deepest ring to the intermediate ring and from the intermediate to the outermost. A1 reused the main-study predictions. A2 recalibrated from scratch and passed the pre-freeze check (false alarms 0.08, 0.10, 0.065; coverage 0.885, 0.88, 0.98) before freezing new predictions. For A3 the attenuation strength was fixed from the model alone as the smallest value on a × 4 \times 4 grid at which the Gaussian posterior standard deviation of central q q kept at least half its prior value ( F = 128,000 F=128{,}000 ); none of the pre-specified grid values { 500 , 2000 , 8000 } \{500,2000,8000\} satisfied the rule, and the grid was extended with the rule unchanged, before any A3 computation on data (a logged deviation). A3 passed the pre-freeze check (false alarms 0.065, 0.06, 0.055; coverage 0.885, 0.86, 0.88). VAE-EKI met all 14 robustness criteria; VAE-Laplace missed 4 (Table 7 , Fig. 5 ). sections.heading: Post-hoc analysis plans.
sections.text: After the main and robustness outcomes were known, seven analysis plans were written, each approved and hash-committed before its own computation and each with outcome descriptions fixed in advance: (1) simpler predictors, the three bootstraps and the attenuation-strength sensitivity; (2) the physics-based comparison at all strengths; (3) the score’s approximations, calibration, adjusted rankings, a noise-only physics baseline and sensitivity to κ \kappa and to the linearisation points; (4) the components of the score and their dependence in the realised systems; (5) the trial-level analysis, the linear-Gaussian reference, the location control, the prior–population check, κ = 1 \kappa=1 and the flagging use; (6) the detection law at the rank of the null covariance, leave-one-slice-out estimates, the agreement of the learned and physics-based scores, flag budgets from 5% to 50%, and the physics-based baseline with κ = 1 \kappa=1 ; (7) refitted bootstrap intervals for the cross-validated log-score gains, their sensitivity to the fold partition, and cross-validation on held-out base slices. One addition after the fifth plan’s results were known, the v1 − - physics difference under bounded reach (computed with the unchanged second-plan code), is logged as a deviation. As a check on ties, Kendall’s τ b \tau_{b} ordered the learned and Gaussian predictions as Spearman’s ρ \rho did in every study and system.

sections.heading: Failed configurations.
sections.text: Three configurations failed the pre-freeze calibration check before the one reported. (1) Contiguous splits. With slices 1–800 for training, 801–900 for calibration and 901–1000 for testing, calibration did not transfer (false alarms 51–68%, coverage 61–74% on the test block): the hidden region was denser in that block (mean q q 0.151 against about 0.11). (2) High-rank model-error covariance. A rank-60 empirical covariance of the decoder’s data-space residuals over-fitted the detector null (false alarms on test 68–75%); the 16-parameter spectrum transferred. (3) Too few slices. With 1,000 slices, false alarms on test were 15–20%; with 2,000, 3–3.5%.

sections.text: Table 11 gives the component analysis. The swap analysis replaces the analytic detection or non-coverage component by its Monte Carlo counterpart; products of per-error means ranked realised blindness like the original score ( ρ \rho within 0.01 of v1). Under bounded reach the Monte Carlo non-coverage probability within reach is below 0.001 for 87–92% of errors (a check on the predictions alone), non-zero mainly for errors with a large effect on q q , which are also the most detectable; within reach, the score built with it ranked realised blindness negatively ( ρ = − 0.05 \rho=-0.05 to − 0.22 -0.22 ).
